HEADLINE: New ACCI head urges big workplace fix
INTRO: The Coalition needs an election workplace relations policy that responds to the "incredible" over-regulation of workplaces and helps businesses "drowning in red tape", says the new head of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
TEXT:
The Coalition needs an election workplace relations policy that responds to the "incredible" over-regulation of workplaces and helps businesses "drowning in red tape", says the new head of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

James Pearson, who has succeeded Kate Carnell as the chamber's chief executive, said the Coalition and the Labor Party should not be afraid of advocating "reasonable and pragmatic" changes to the federal workplace laws.

In one of his first public outings, Mr Pearson will debate ACTU secretary Dave Oliver at the National Press Club in Canberra on Tuesday on the future of employment in Australia.

A former executive with Shell Australia, Mr Pearson, 56, was previously chief executive of the chamber's Western Australian division. He has held executive positions with Chevron Australia, the Australian Petroleum Production & Exploration Association, the Western Australian Department of Resources Development and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

He said he started his full-time working career during the Accord era where collaboration by employers and unions was facilitated by the Hawke and Keating governments.

But the father of three said the workplace relations debate had been polarised for some years, with any proposal for moderate change depicted by unions as a return to John Howard's WorkChoices regime.

"The fact is workplace relations is one of the areas where the country performs worst in terms of its global competitiveness," he said on Monday.

"We ought to be able to debate these issues robustly without the union movement resorting to that old tired ghost story about any attempt at reasonable industrial relations reform in Australia being a return to WorkChoices. The fact is that is simply a ghost story used by the union movement to try and scare the pants off the latest generation of politicians.

"My organisation, which is the largest and most representative business network in the country, is determined to prosecute the case for sound, reasonable, pragmatic reform that will give our generation and our children an opportunity to enjoy at least as high living standards as we do."

Mr Pearson said the Coalition and the Labor opposition should not be afraid of workplace policy change.

"Australian workplaces are incredibly over-regulated," he said. "Businesses, and our members tell us this all the time, are drowning in red tape. We have done surveys that show a quarter of our members are spending 11 hours or more a week on compliance, with an annual cost for half of them at $10,000."

He reiterated the chamber's support for cutting Sunday penalty rates to the lesser rates paid on Saturday. "Here is yet another tired example of where the union movement will verbal anyone whose position is different from their orthodox line," he said, arguing that cutting penalties would lead to more businesses opening on Sundays.

He also lashed out at unions for depicting the government's internship scheme as "$4-an-hour jobs".

"They completely and deliberately ignore the fact that young jobless going into the scheme will be receiving their Newstart entitlement, they will still receive their income support at the full rate, and on top of that they will be paid $200 a fortnight for working up to 25 hours a week," he said.

His comments came as the Fair Work Commission was due to hand down its annual minimum wage decision on Tuesday.

A commission full bench earlier overturned a March ruling that restricted construction union officials exercising their rights to enter workplaces in three states.

Key points

Chief says over-regulation in workplaces and business red tape need fixing.

Unions resort to 'tired' WorkChoices 'ghost story'.

HEADLINE: This start-up doesn't need a board or CEO
INTRO: The biggest crowdfunding project ever launched to find new businesses has no strategy, no board or CEO, and is run entirely by computer code. Even its founder acknowledges that its legal rights will be tenuous.
TEXT:
The biggest crowdfunding project ever launched to find new businesses has no strategy, no board or CEO, and is run entirely by computer code. Even its founder acknowledges that its legal rights will be tenuous.

Yet Australian investors and organisations were among hundreds of backers of this new organisation, known as the Decentralised Autonomous Organisation or DAO, and probably best described as an online co-operative.

It raised $US132 million ($184 million) over the weekend from speculative investors like Hugo O'Connor, the head of innovation at Bit Trade Australia. Other local investors include smaller research organisations hoping to build on the technology for their own operations.

"A decentralised autonomous organisation is about redistributing power to the collective pool of people, rather than a central point," Mr O'Connor said.

"We are trying to systematise the organising of groups of people sharing common skills or interests. Guilds, co-operatives and friendly societies share many of these ideas which until now have not been formalised in software."

DAO's owners each receive voting rights on how it should operate. Each participant buys tokens representing their say.

A group can program what the entity should do at what time and is designed to be a democratically driven vehicle.

The organisation, now in control of $US150 million worth of ether, hopes to deploy its capital to Ethereum-based projects and in turn generate income.

Ethereum is best described as a cousin of the blockchain.

Whereas the blockchain is a decentralised network of computers that transfers money (or bitcoin), Ethereum allows software programs to run.

Like many start-ups, it seems more into creating or funding projects with a compelling theorum.

Technology liftout

HEADLINE: Morrison worried about growth
INTRO: Treasurer Scott Morrison is ramping up attacks on Labor's opposition to corporate tax cuts in anticipation figures this week will show economic growth slowed last quarter.
TEXT:
Treasurer Scott Morrison is ramping up attacks on Labor's opposition to corporate tax cuts in anticipation figures this week will show economic growth slowed last quarter.

Speaking after profits from mining to manufacturing and property services tanked by almost 5 per cent in the March quarter - escalating concerns about the sustainability of share investor dividend expectations - Mr Morrison indicated Wednesday's national accounts were likely to underscore the economy's fragility.

"This is a very sensitive time for the Australian economy," he said in an interview. "Wherever the figures land, the policy objective doesn't change - and that's about securing growth in this economy. You can't increase investment by taxing it more."

The Coalition's pre-emptive attack on Labor underscores the political importance of this week's gross domestic product figures, which are expected to show the economy slowed to a below-trend 2.7 per cent in the first quarter from 3 per cent last year. Quarterly GDP growth stalled at 0.6 per cent in the three months ended March 31, economists say.

Shadow treasurer Chris Bowen said the government's election campaign now amounts to a combination of "forget the last three years" and a business tax cut that "delivers a tiny 0.1 per cent of GDP growth a year".

"The government is so incompetent it thinks its $50 billion tax handout for big business, which won't eventuate for 10 years, is the answer to solving its own short-term economic failures," Mr Bowen said.

Despite record-low official interest rates and a weaker dollar - which traded close to a three-month low at US71.61¢ on Monday - investment outside the resources sector is unable to offset the drag from the fading mining boom.

Led by a 9.6 per cent collapse in mining profits to levels last seen in 2004, total profits fell 4.7 per cent, missing expectations of no change. Manufacturing fell 14.5 per cent, and property and business services slid 6.4 per cent. Total wages and salaries rose 3.5 per cent.

"We are in a very difficult economic environment, part of which is what we're seeing on wages and profits," Mr Morrison said. "A lot of this stuff has been very modest."

The weak profit figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics follow seven weeks of gains on the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 stock index, prompting some analysts to predict the current rally will peter out.

"The market's run as far as it's going to, unless we get further upside to the earnings outlook," said Perpetual Investments head of investment strategy Matt Sherwood.

Mr Morrison acknowledged the weakness in non-mining investment, saying it was the "one area that has been lagging and I think frustrating all of us - and [Reserve Bank of Australia governor] Glenn Stevens talks about this a lot. "Which is why we have got to do things that influence investment in that sector," he said.

Mr Morrison said there was a "stability X-factor" that businesses were seeking from Canberra's policy settings and which is threatened by Labor's fight against lower corporate taxes and its plans to curb negative gearing.

"If Labor were elected and introduced negative gearing changes that would obviously have an impact on the value of homes and therefore confidence and consumption," he said.

"Whilst there are plenty of reasons that's a daft idea, the key economic impact on consumer confidence alone should be good enough reason not to go down this path."

Mr Morrison criticised Opposition Leader Bill Shorten for ignoring the growth likely to emerge from a corporate tax cut. "This is a bloke who is dismissing growth. Apparently a 1 per cent lift in growth is something he's prepared to throw away," he said.

"In this economy you fight for every inch of growth, just like every business fights for every inch of profit."

He predicted Mr Shorten wouldn't encourage more investment in the economy by comparing small and medium-sized businesses to "multinationals and accusing them of being a drain on the economy or budget.

"These are people who mortgaged their homes to build their companies," he said.

HEADLINE: Labor's decade of 49pc tax
SUBHEAD: Shorten to keep 'temporary' deficit levy long term
INTRO: Australians could be saddled with a top marginal income tax rate of 49 per cent for a decade after leader Bill Shorten confirmed Labor would keep the Coalition's "temporary" deficit levy for at least 10 years to pay for hospitals.
TEXT:
Australians could be saddled with a top marginal income tax rate of 49 per cent for a decade after leader Bill Shorten confirmed Labor would keep the Coalition's "temporary" deficit levy for at least 10 years to pay for hospitals.

During Sunday night's leaders' debate with Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, Mr Shorten said that closer to the election when Labor announced its hospital-funding policy, he would replace a "significant dimension" of the $57 billion in federal funding that was cut by the Abbott government in the 2014 budget.

"We can afford to do what I just said because we're not going to hand out $17 billion to the top 3 per cent of income earners over the next 10 years because we will do budget repair that is fair," the Labor leader said.

A Labor spokesman confirmed that Mr Shorten was referring to the so-called temporary budget repair levy, also introduced in the 2014 budget, which added 2 percentage points to the top marginal tax rate that applies to income of over $180,000.

It was legislated to apply for three years and is scheduled to expire on July 1 next year. Labor has already promised to keep the levy, claiming it was needed because the budget was still in deficit, but Mr Shorten's statement was the first time he has nominated for how long it should stay.

Keeping the levy will raise $4.2 billion over the four years to 2019-20 while Mr Shorten's statement suggests Labor has had the tax costed for a decade.

It will supplement Labor's boost to hospital funding by not going ahead with the bulk of the scheduled cuts to company tax which are budgeted to cost $48 billion over the decade. Labor will support only dropping the corporate rate from 28.5 per cent to 27.5 per cent for businesses with turnovers up to $2 million.

Mr Shorten's declaration that the levy will last at least another decade makes it effectively permanent and further sharpens the lines of this election campaign, with Labor championing the funding of essential services such as health and education ahead of giving tax cuts to big business and high-income earners.

On Monday night, Seven News reported Mr Shorten will launch Labor's campaign in the western Sydney seat of Lindsay, not the usual location of Brisbane.

In recent days, he has sharpened his attacks on the company tax cuts, saying the government was not serious about them because they were only formulated after its GST plans fell over. He said the big banks did not deserve a $7.4 billion slice of the cuts. The big banks disagreed.

"In our response to the federal government's tax discussion paper in June 2015, the Australian Bankers' Association noted that the single most important economic reform to promote investment, growth and jobs is to cut the company tax rate. This position remains unchanged," the banks' lobby group said.

If Labors wins the July 2 election it will have to pass legislation to keep the levy, which is due to expire automatically. This should not be a problem because the Greens, who will have a balance of power in the Senate after he election, believe the levy should be permanent and would be expected to pass Labor's legislation.

The levy was introduced, in part, to raise money but was also a political tactic to assuage the anger of those in lower incomes who bore the brunt of the cuts in the now-notorious 2014 budget.

Business railed against it on the basis that it rendered Australia's uncompetitive top tax rate even more so, making investment harder to attract, a point then Treasurer Joe Hockey later acknowledged.

During Friday's Treasurers' debate, both Scott Morrison and shadow treasurer Chris Bowen were asked whether they were concerned there would be an increase in "creative accounting" given the widening differential between Australia's top marginal tax rate and a new lower company tax rate of 27.5 per cent as high income earners restructured their affairs.

Mr Morrison said the gap would be smaller under the Coalition while Mr Bowen blamed the government.

"With the budget under pressure, now is not the time to take the top marginal rate back down," he said.

"If it was important for budget repair three years ago and the deficit has tripled, it's even more important now. The top marginal tax rate shouldn't be the only one that is temporary.

"That's the way we see it. It is about priorities and we didn't make this decision lightly or for fun but it's the right decision for the times."

HEADLINE: Corporate profits down 4.7 pc
INTRO: Corporate profits continued to decline in the March quarter, adding some drag to the value of national output ahead of Wednesday's gross domestic product figures.
TEXT:
Corporate profits continued to decline in the March quarter, adding some drag to the value of national output ahead of Wednesday's gross domestic product figures.

The data, which came in below expectations, also point to future patchiness in company profits.

After watching seven weeks of gains on the main S&P/ASX200 index, equity analysts have started to warn that the current rally has run its course.

"The market's run as far as it's going to, unless we get further upside to the earnings outlook," said Perpetual Investments' head of investment strategy Matt Sherwood.

The maturity of the US bull market, added to jitters in the lead-up to Australia's election were also reasons for caution, said Geoff Wilson of Wilson Asset Management. "The overall economy has slowed and the next couple of months is going to be difficult for the domestic economy until the election is over and that uncertainty is over," he said.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that gross operating profits declined 4.7 per cent in the first three months of the year, seasonally adjusted, for a year-on-year decline of 8.4 per cent.

The figure was worse than expected, and the dollar dipped slightly, to around US71.56¢. In late local trade it was buying US71.60¢, compared with US72.25¢ at the same time on Friday.

However, the value of inventories, whose volatility can also blindside GDP estimates, rose 0.4 per cent for the quarter, above expectations of zero.

Although piled-up inventories can reflect slow or weak sales, their accumulated value goes to the positive side of the national accounts ledger.

UBS noted this, and said a 1.2 per cent quarterly increase in sales would also be positive for one measure of GDP.

However, the bank also noted it wasn't just mining-related profits that continued to slide; non-mining industries were also weak, down 3.1 per cent for the quarter and 3.3 per cent for the year.

Most of this decline was concentrated in manufacturing, a sector that was supposed to benefit from a lower Australian dollar, and finance and insurance services.

One of the stellar performers, by contrast, was the real estate industry, whose profit margin of 49.8 per cent was the widest of all sub-sectors. Tourism and food services also fared well.

Some analysts pointed to this as proof the transition away from mining-related investment to growth from residential housing development and services exports is well under way.

However, the low profitability seen in many industries chimed with the disappointing first quarter-business investment data released last week. This could augur badly for the current and future quarters, said ANZ Banking's head of Australian economics Felicity Emmett.

"Historically, you can see quite a good relationship between profit and investment," she said. "As the good times come along, companies feel confident about investing more in future growth."

After a surprisingly robust 0.6 per cent expansion in the final quarter of 2015, GDP growth is expected to come in again at 0.6 per cent for the first three months of the year, according to a Bloomberg survey of economists.

This, however, will reduce the year-on-year growth rate to 2.7 per cent from 3 per cent at the end of last year.

Economists expect net exports to have provided much of the growth, with greater volumes compensating for a slight fall in the terms of trade, which measures the value of exports against the cost of imports.

HEADLINE: Labor to raid $5b fund to develop tourism in northern Australia
INTRO: Tourism is one of the biggest employers in northern Australia and is growing. Bill Shorten, Opposition Leader
TEXT:
Labor will "redirect" $1 billion from the government's $5 billion loan scheme for the development of northern Australia and devote it specifically to tourism infrastructure and other investments in the top end, Bill Shorten will announce on Tuesday.

Campaigning in northern Queensland for a second successive day on Tuesday, Mr Shorten will promise to redirect one-fifth of the money if elected to "help northern Australia build the tourism infrastructure it needs to harness the huge economic potential of the Asian tourism boom".

"Tourism is one of the biggest employers in northern Australia and is growing. But the lack of high-quality facilities will limit Australia's ability to capture and grow our share of the booming Asian travel market unless we invest today," he will say.

"By 2030 there will be over 3 billion people in the Asian middle classes seeking international tourism opportunities in our region and beyond. We want them to choose Australia."

The reallocated $1 billion will be put in a Northern Australia Tourism Infrastructure Fund, to boost partnerships with the tourism sector and provide incentives for investment in new and upgraded tourism infrastructure.

The policy will not add further to Labor's spending commitments because it will be reallocating money already budgeted.

Following its white paper on Developing Northern Australia, the Coalition government established a $5 billion Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility. From July 1, this year, it will fund concessional loans to "encourage and complement private sector investment in economic infrastructure that otherwise would not be built or would not be built for some time" in the nation's north.

The Coalition fund would be administered by a seven-member independent board chaired by Sharon Warburton.

Labor's fund will be administered by a renewed Department of Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism.

Mr Shorten's announcement follows Monday's trip to the Great Barrier Reef where he pledged almost $500 million to try to protect the ailing wonder.

The Opposition Leader pledged $377 million of new funding in a $500 million grant over five years for science and research as well as reef management.

Mr Shorten and Malcolm Turnbull on Monday both claimed to be the biggest defenders of the reef as a new report showed coral bleaching was worse than previously thought. It shows mass coral bleaching had destroyed as much as 35 per cent of the northern and central Great Barrier Reef.

The study of 84 reefs by the ARC Centre of Excellence for Coral Reef Studies at James Cook University found that only 7 per cent of the reef, mostly in southern parts, had avoided any major damage.

Professor Terry Hughes, of the ARC, said they were caught by surprise by the extent of the damage, which was worse than previous bleaching events in 1998 and 2002.

Mr Shorten said Labor was spending the money because the "this reef is worth saving".

"If we do not act, it is in serious danger of being irreparably damaged. If we do not act, our children will rightly ask us why didn't we. This is not a problem that I'm inclined to pass on to future generations," he said.

HEADLINE: Flaws in ciggies tax collection
INTRO: An audit report has identified serious shortcomings in the collection of taxes on imported tobacco products, which are worth about $8 billion a year.
TEXT:
An audit report has identified serious shortcomings in the collection of taxes on imported tobacco products, which are worth about $8 billion a year.

Both political parties plan to use increases in tobacco excise to pay for spending promises, but the damning Australian National Audit Office report finds the system is so broken "there is limited assurance that the correct amount of tobacco customs duty is being collected and reported".

Moreover, federal budget revenue estimates are unreliable because they do not factor in the illicit tobacco trade.

"There is uncertainty about forward estimates of tobacco revenue, as these estimates do not incorporate a change in supply and demand of dutiable tobacco arising from cheaper illicit product," the report says.

In the five years to 2014-15, the government collected an average of $8.1 billion in tobacco excise and customs duty each year.

The Australian Taxation Office and Department of Immigration and Border Protection jointly manage the movement and storage of tobacco through licensed warehouses.

The goods, which are referred to as underbond, are stored in these warehouses until they are released for home consumption, moved to duty-free outlets or exported.

But the ANAO report found there were few checks and balances in place.

"The administration of tobacco excise equivalent goods and the collection of customs duty has fallen short of effective practice," it said.

Importers are required to self-report the duty owed on tobacco products.

But the risk of non-compliance was assessed by the ATO as ranging from "moderate" in 2011 to "significant" in 2015, when there was "an observed increase in the number of entities displaying non-compliant behaviour that are importing tobacco and/or storing imported tobacco".

"The ATO advised that the reason for the changed risk ratings over the years is largely a consequence of shifts in focus brought by different ATO managers when scoping risk assessments," the report said.

"Most recently, the raising of the risk to 'significant' was driven by the reputational risk for the ATO and DIBP as a result of large seizures of illicit tobacco ... and a noted increase in the incidence of theft from smaller warehouses, which account for approximately 2 per cent of the revenue collected."

The federal budget included four annual increases in tobacco excise of 12.5 per cent per year from 2017 until 2020, saving $4.7 billion over the forward estimates.

Labor earlier announced a policy to save $47.7 billion over 10 years by increasing tobacco excise until 2020 to fund health and education policies.

But analysts questioned if tobacco revenue, which is being undermined by falling smoking rates, would keep pace over the longer term with the faster-growing policies it would have to pay for.

Stephen Bartos, Parliamentary Budget Officer for the NSW Parliament between September 2014 and July 2015, said accurately estimating the revenue impact was "really tricky".

"Obviously there will be a point at which you raise tobacco excise so much that everyone stops smoking and you raise no money," he said.

Similarly, nobody knows what effect illicit tobacco supply will have.

The ANAO report said budget assumptions did not "factor in the size of the illicit trade in tobacco and potential changes to the supply of and demand for dutiable goods as a result of the increase in costs in the legitimate market".

HEADLINE: Sydney home prices lead way with 3.4pc surge
INTRO: Sydney home prices led a national rise this month in line with April's increase, research firm CoreLogic said.
TEXT:
Sydney home prices led a national rise this month in line with April's increase, research firm CoreLogic said.

A 3.4 per cent increase in the NSW capital this month helped drive the capital city-average index 1.6 per cent at the same time, the data provider said, up from 1.7 per cent last month.

"It looks as if the upcoming election and debate around taxation policy hasn't been enough to dampen the renewed bounce in home values, with the pace of capital appreciation in the housing market surging in May, largely driven by a bounce in Sydney home values," CoreLogic head of research Tim Lawless said.

The figures suggest a revving up of the NSW housing market that started the year slowly, when there were initial monthly gains of 0.5 per cent that accelerated to 1 per cent then 2.4 per cent.

CoreLogic's preview of the month-end figures came a day after a strong weekend result that had Sydney and Melbourne chalk up auction clearance rates in the mid 70 per cent range, sparked, in part, by concerns that negative gearing tax concessions on property sales might be reduced after the July 2 federal election.

Other people are more cautious about the overall rate of gain, questioning if the market - parts of which are pulling their heads in in a bout of pre-election caution - is rising that fast.

"I do suggest the market in Sydney has stabilised, but it's not rising at that rate," said Louis Christopher, the head of rival SQM Research.

"It's stabilised, as a result of rate cut we had, as a result of APRA actions last year that have gone through the market and the market's no longer responding to that as much as it was."

Separate figures published by the Housing Industry Association on Monday painted a different picture of a slowdown in NSW, where new home sales fell 8.1 per cent in April to 1260 - 4 per cent below the monthly average throughout 2015 - to their lowest monthly figure since May last year.

NSW wasn't alone. Victoria was the only state to chalk up an increase in new sales of detached houses in April.

Overall new home sales fell 4.7 per cent in April as sales of so-called multi-unit dwellings dropped 10.8 per cent from March and stand alone homes fell 3 per cent, the HIA said.

April's total of 7610 new dwellings sold, based on figures from the largest volume builders, was down from 7986 in March.

"The trend in new home sales reiterates that the peak for the cycle has passed, but the descent we're now observing is very mild," said HIA economist Diwa Hopkins. "This signals the potential for very healthy home construction activity throughout 2016, much as we have been anticipating."
